The ordinance authorizes solar-generation public improvements and contracts.

Official sponsorship record. Sponsorship is not converted into an ideology score.
The people who receive service, pay rates, and can participate in public decisions.
City offices, council, budgets, and public utilities.
The entities that serve customers, buy power, and manage distribution.
Wholesale markets, transmission, and power-purchase relationships.
Generation assets and the companies that own or operate them.
State and federal bodies that regulate safety, rates, markets, and pollution.
Residents receive electricity service, pay bills or rates, and can influence public decisions through elections, hearings, comments, and public records requests.
The mayor leads city administration. The office does not set every regional electricity-market rule, but it connects to city-owned utility administration and local policy.
Council can pass local ordinances, approve appropriations, hold hearings, and authorize public actions when the charter or law gives it that role.
The department manages and supervises Cleveland-owned public utilities, including Cleveland Public Power.
City of Cleveland Department of Public Utilities
Cleveland's municipally owned electric utility. The city describes CPP as serving approximately 74,000 residential, commercial, and industrial customers.
An investor-owned distribution utility serving customers in Northeast Ohio. Its distribution rates and service rules are handled through Ohio utility regulation, not simply by Cleveland City Council.

A public-power partner whose portfolio can include member-owned generation, long-term power contracts, seasonal purchases, and market purchases. Cleveland participation must be verified agreement by agreement.
PJM operates a competitive wholesale electricity market and manages the reliability of its regional transmission grid. It is not a Cleveland department.
Regional transmission and wholesale market footprint
A regional nuclear generating asset. The map separates plant ownership, licensed operation, electricity contracts, grid dispatch, and nuclear safety oversight.
U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission reactor records
A regional nuclear generating asset near Oak Harbor. The NRC is the safety and licensing authority; market dispatch and electricity contracts are separate relationships.
Ohio's utility regulator. It oversees rates and distribution regulation for investor-owned utilities, including matters affecting Cleveland customers of The Illuminating Company.
Federal oversight for interstate wholesale electricity markets and transmission rules. FERC does not run Cleveland's retail utility counter.
Federal nuclear safety and licensing authority. It is separate from the plant owner, operator, utility buyer, and grid market.

A contract-level record should identify the buyer, seller, facility, term, quantity, price, amendments, exit terms, authorizing vote, and resident rate impact. The public prototype marks the contract inventory as incomplete until each agreement is verified.
CPP is the city-owned utility relationship to trace.
Some Cleveland customers are served through the investor-owned distribution system.
Council actions can authorize local budgets, ordinances, and public contracts when legally required.
The department manages and supervises city-owned utilities.
AMP participation must be verified contract by contract; membership alone is not proof of every project.
Contract pages connect public approvals to financial obligations.
PUCO is the state utility-regulatory relationship for investor-owned distribution rates.
Wholesale market and transmission relationships are distinct from local retail service.
Grid dispatch is not the same as ownership or a Cleveland contract.
NRC handles nuclear safety and licensing.
FERC oversees interstate wholesale-market and transmission rules.
State retail distribution and federal wholesale authority are different layers.
The children, caregivers, and communities the system is supposed to serve.
CMSD, its board, CEO, schools, and district decisions.
The mayoral appointment path, levies, bonds, facilities, and public votes.
State funding, report cards, standards, authorizers, and state law.
Federal funding, civil-rights protections, privacy, and program rules.
Charter sponsors, labor, vendors, facilities, and community partners.
Students and families experience the school system directly. They can participate through enrollment, board meetings, public comment, voting on levies and bonds, and formal complaint or appeal paths.
Cleveland Metropolitan School District and connected public-school options
Cleveland's public school district. The map treats the district as an institution, then separates the board, CEO, funding decisions, schools, labor, and state or federal rules connected to it.
The board is the public decision body for district governance. Board packets and meeting records are where families can follow agendas, resolutions, budgets, and votes.
The district's CEO leads administration and operations. A leader profile should show documented responsibilities and decisions, not infer personal beliefs from a single policy or vote.

Levies and bonds are public-finance decisions that can affect operating money, buildings, debt, and long-term obligations. Each record should connect to the ballot language, vote, amount, term, and affected schools.
Cuyahoga County Board of Elections / CMSD records

Cleveland's mayoral role in appointing CMSD board members is a governance connection that should be shown with the appointment record and the board's public duties, not as total control over the district.
Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
The state education agency connects to school funding, report cards, standards, federal-program administration, and school or district requirements.
Ohio community schools are public, tuition-free, and independent of traditional districts. Their sponsors and operators are a separate relationship that families should be able to inspect.
Ohio Department of Education community schools
Collective-bargaining agreements shape working conditions, staffing, pay, and school operations. The map should link the current agreement and any board action that approves it.
The federal layer administers and coordinates many forms of education assistance and protects rights through programs and laws. It does not run Cleveland schools day to day.
Federal programs can provide targeted support, including programs for students with disabilities, students in poverty, and other protected or underserved groups.
Construction, transportation, food, technology, and facilities contracts can move significant public money. Each vendor relationship needs a contract, authorization, term, and performance record.
Vendor and contract registry to be verified
CMSD is the local public-school institution to trace.
Board records show public governance actions.
The board and CEO are distinct governance and administration roles.
Levy, bond, budget, and school decisions should resolve to records.
The appointment record shows a connection, not total control.
State rules and funding are a separate layer from district administration.
Ohio school-funding records connect state money to district finance.
Community schools are independent public-school relationships, not CMSD departments.
Collective bargaining should be linked to the agreement and board record.
State and federal program administration are connected but not identical.
Federal programs distribute targeted education support.
Procurement records are needed to trace public spending.
An agenda entry establishes consideration, not proof of passage or an executed contract.
One of the two chambers of Ohio’s legislature. Members consider state bills and represent Ohio House districts.
The other chamber of Ohio’s legislature. Its districts are different from city wards and Ohio House districts.
One chamber of Congress. House members represent congressional districts.
One chamber of Congress. U.S. senators represent states. The Senate has its own responsibilities within the federal system.
The county’s legislative branch is separate from Cleveland City Council. Residents elect members by county council district.
The county executive leads county administration, separately from Cleveland’s mayor.
Ohio Revised Code 1901.01 establishes municipal courts, including Cleveland Municipal Court. Court authority is not merely a city department reporting line.
RTA runs the regional transit system. Its board approves policies, budgets, and major contracts. Bus service and city street maintenance have different decision paths.
The board sets policy, oversees management, and approves the budget. Residents may comment at board meetings; committee meetings have different comment rules.
The Ohio House and Senate consider state bills. A bill must follow the state legislative process before becoming law.
The governor leads Ohio’s executive branch. State authority is distinct from Cleveland’s mayor and council.
The U.S. House and Senate make federal laws through the federal legislative process. Congressional districts are different from city wards.
County government serves Cleveland and other communities in Cuyahoga County. Its offices are separate from Cleveland City Hall.
Ohio EPA administers state environmental programs and permits. The responsible agency depends on the type of pollution or permit.
